title: How AAC gives Julia an extra voice
description:
What happens when speech isn’t always available?
 
Julia, an autistic adult and AAC user, shares how AAC gives her an extra voice when speech doesn’t work.

Too often, AAC is seen as a last resort. In reality, many more people could benefit from it.

#AutismAcceptanceMonth #AssistiveWare #Proloquo #MoretoSay

title: Let's move under the sea - brain break
description:
To watch more AAC videos like this, visit: https://www.assistiveware.com/resources?category=classroom-aac-modeling

Let's move under the sea!
This Brain Break video gets everyone walking, swimming, and reaching while modeling AAC movement words.

Brain breaks are short, intentional pauses that help children refocus and recharge. These quick breaks support children’s concentration, learning, and well-being, while also reducing restlessness.

Brain breaks fit easily into daily home routines and classroom routines. They offer a fun, consistent way to model AAC in an engaging, repeatable way, supporting language development for all learners.

title: The Mountains of Echolalia
description:
Echolalia is a natural part of autistic communication. It means "echo speech," and it can be either immediate or delayed. For many autistic people with limited speech, delayed echolalia is a primary way to communicate.

This Autism Acceptance Month, listen to the voices around you, including those using AAC, and find joy in the echoes. Echoing with AAC is just as much echolalia as echoing with speech.

Explore the full Land of Autistic Communication here: https://www.assistiveware.com/autism-acceptance-communication

title: Let's move on the jumping castle - brain break
description:
To watch more AAC videos like this, visit: https://www.assistiveware.com/resources?category=classroom-aac-modeling

Jump, move, and turn on the jumping castle!
This joyful Brain Beak video models movement words and gets everyone bouncing with excitement.

Brain breaks are short, intentional pauses that help children refocus and recharge. These quick breaks support children’s concentration, learning, and well-being, while also reducing restlessness.

Brain breaks fit easily into daily home routines and classroom routines. They offer a fun, consistent way to model AAC in an engaging, repeatable way, supporting language development for all learners.

description:
Watch the story of Jay and Nick - identical twins diagnosed with autism. Nick started speaking at the age of three, while Jay did not. They were separated into different classrooms at kindergarten - Nick joined a mainstream class, while Jay was placed in a self-contained classroom. Jay's learning gap with Nick grew because he was not exposed to the same things.

Jay's story is a testament to the power of AAC, not only in developing language and communication, but fostering understanding and inclusion in the communication partners around a non-speaking child.

description:
In this Facebook live, Amanda reads "What's in the Witch's Kitchen?" by Nick Sharatt. The session includes AAC modelling, and writing a list of rhyming words! Amanda models on Proloquo.

This is a Facebook live video recorded in October 2023. Find us on Facebook at: https://www.facebook.com/AssistiveWare

Proloquo is a new, groundbreaking AAC app designed for nonspeaking children and adults learning language through AAC.

Learn more about our next generation AAC solution as seen in this video: https://www.assistiveware.com/products/proloquo

This is a Facebook live video recorded in September 2023. Find us on Facebook at: https://www.facebook.com/AssistiveWare

Proloquo is a new, groundbreaking AAC app designed for nonspeaking children and adults learning language through AAC.

Learn more about our next generation AAC solution as seen in this video: https://www.assistiveware.com/products/proloquo

Learning time management can be fun with our clock countdowns! These clock countdowns can be used in a variety of ways. Here are some of our favorites:

2️⃣ Smooth transitions after recess: The clock countdowns act as a visual cue, signaling the end of the break. It helps students refocus their attention and prepares them for the upcoming lesson helping for a seamless transition between recess and class time.

3️⃣ Engaging classroom breaks: These countdowns empower students to become more time-conscious. By fostering a sense of responsibility and awareness, countdowns help students make the most of their valuable classroom moments and develop essential time management skills. 

Let the countdown begin! 🚀✨

description:
🕒 Interactive clock countdown for elementary school students! ⏰ 

Learning time management can be fun with our clock countdowns! These clock countdowns can be used in a variety of ways. Here are some of our favorites: 

1️⃣ Energize class activities: Use the clock countdown to time different classroom exercises, like group discussions, classroom games, and personal work time. 

2️⃣ Smooth transitions after recess: The clock countdowns act as a visual cue, signaling the end of the break. It helps students refocus their attention and prepares them for the upcoming lesson helping for a seamless transition between recess and class time.

3️⃣ Engaging classroom breaks: These countdowns empower students to become more time-conscious. By fostering a sense of responsibility and awareness, countdowns help students make the most of their valuable classroom moments and develop essential time management skills. 

Let the countdown begin! 🚀✨

🕒 Interactive clock countdown for elementary school students! ⏰ 

Learning time management can be fun with our clock countdowns! These clock countdowns can be used in a variety of ways. Here are some of our favorites: 

1️⃣ Energize class activities: Use the clock countdown to time different classroom exercises, like group discussions, classroom games, and personal work time. 

2️⃣ Smooth transitions after recess: The clock countdowns act as a visual cue, signaling the end of the break. It helps students refocus their attention and prepares them for the upcoming lesson helping for a seamless transition between recess and class time.

3️⃣ Engaging classroom breaks: These countdowns empower students to become more time-conscious. By fostering a sense of responsibility and awareness, countdowns help students make the most of their valuable classroom moments and develop essential time management skills. 

Let the countdown begin! 🚀✨

3️⃣ Engaging classroom breaks: These countdowns empower students to become more time-conscious. By fostering a sense of responsibility and awareness, countdowns help students make the most of their valuable classroom moments and develop essential time management skills.

description:
🕒 Interactive clock countdown for middle school students! ⏰ 

Learning time management can be fun with our clock countdowns! These clock countdowns can be used in a variety of ways. Here are some of our favorites: 

1️⃣ Energize class activities: Use the clock countdown to time different classroom exercises, like group discussions, classroom games, and personal work time. 

2️⃣ Smooth transitions after breaks: The clock countdowns act as a visual cue, signaling the end of the break. It helps students refocus their attention and prepares them for the upcoming lesson helping for a seamless transition between break and class time.

3️⃣ Engaging classroom breaks: These countdowns empower students to become more time-conscious. By fostering a sense of responsibility and awareness, countdowns help students make the most of their valuable classroom moments and develop essential time management skills. 

Let the countdown begin! 🚀

Learning time management can be fun with our clock countdowns! These clock countdowns can be used in a variety of ways. Here are some of our favorites: 

1️⃣ Energize class activities: Use the clock countdown to time different classroom exercises, like group discussions, classroom games, and personal work time. 

2️⃣ Smooth transitions after recess: The clock countdowns act as a visual cue, signaling the end of the break. It helps students refocus their attention and prepares them for the upcoming lesson helping for a seamless transition between recess and class time.

3️⃣ Engaging classroom breaks: These countdowns empower students to become more time-conscious. By fostering a sense of responsibility and awareness, countdowns help students make the most of their valuable classroom moments and develop essential time management skills. 

Let the countdown begin! 🚀✨

🕒 Interactive clock countdown for elementary and middle school students! ⏰ 

Learning time management can be fun with our clock countdowns! These clock countdowns can be used in a variety of ways. Here are some of our favorites: 

1️⃣ Energize class activities: Use the clock countdown to time different classroom exercises, like group discussions, classroom games, and personal work time. 

2️⃣ Smooth transitions after recess: The clock countdowns act as a visual cue, signaling the end of the break. It helps students refocus their attention and prepares them for the upcoming lesson helping for a seamless transition between recess and class time.

3️⃣ Engaging classroom breaks: These countdowns empower students to become more time-conscious. By fostering a sense of responsibility and awareness, countdowns help students make the most of their valuable classroom moments and develop essential time management skills. 

Let the countdown begin! 🚀✨

Proloquo is a new, groundbreaking AAC app designed for nonspeaking children and adults learning language through AAC.

Learn more about our next generation AAC solution as seen in this video: https://www.assistiveware.com/products/proloquo

title: Using AAC for an improv show
description:
Check out this AAC Improv show directed by one of our team members, Alyssa Hillary Zisk, in Rhode Island. The show was part of the Contemporary Theater Company's 2023 Springboard Season and showed actors using AAC to communicate on stage. https://www.contemporarytheatercompany.com/

AssistiveWare provided Proloquo licenses for the show. Learn more about Proloquo here: https://www.assistiveware.com/products/proloquo

Would you like to start a similar initiative at home? Don’t hesitate to reach out to us!

title: Autism Acceptance Month - You Are Not Broken
description:
For Autism Acceptance Month 2023 watch a short message from Cole Sorensen - an Autistic AAC user, to his younger self.
Cole reminds us that there is nothing inherently broken about us. Being autistic means existing in the world in a different way. 

What would you like to tell your younger self?

Thank you, Cole, for your wise words.

Read Cole's blog: https://assistivewa.re/40Gmitx

description:
In this Facebook live, Amanda reads "Once Upon a Time". The session includes AAC modelling, some wish making and even some magic! Amanda models on Proloquo.

This is a Facebook live video recorded in October 2022. Find us on Facebook at: https://www.facebook.com/AssistiveWare

Proloquo is a new, groundbreaking AAC app designed for nonspeaking children and adults learning language through AAC.

Learn more about our next generation AAC solution as seen in this video: https://www.assistiveware.com/products/proloquo

title: AAC, literacy, and fun Just Add Glitter
description:
In this Facebook live, Amanda reads the book "Just Add Glitter". The session includes AAC modelling during the book reading, writing a list and making a card. Amanda models on Proloquo2Go and a core word board.

This is a Facebook live video recorded in April 2022. Find us on Facebook at: https://www.facebook.com/AssistiveWare

What is AAC? https://www.assistiveware.com/learn-aac/what-is-aac

description:
What is it like to be autistic and non-speaking in a world that has already made up its mind about you? 

This Is Not About Me tells the story of Jordyn Zimmerman. As a child Jordyn dreamt of becoming a teacher. Unable to communicate, teachers thought she was also unable to understand or learn. Year after year, her behavior worsened. Jordyn found herself caught in a system that unintentionally turned her life into a living nightmare. Finally, at the age of 18, with the help of educators who see her differently, she manages to turn her fate and flourish.

Watch the story of one autistic woman that fought hard to be recognized and trusted. Share the trailer to bring awareness and change the lives of countless others fighting that same system today. https://thisisnotaboutme.film

Trigger warning: This documentary includes conversations about and references to restraint and topics such as disability-based discrimination and harassment. We acknowledge that this content may be difficult to view, so we encourage you to prepare emotionally before proceeding. Take care of your safety and well-being. If purchasing the movie for someone other than yourself, please share this message with them.

As the author of the blog, Amanda talks about "5 ways you can support AAC users to participate in conversation" in this video. 
AAC users can face some challenges in speaking up in day-to-day conversations. Learn how to support and encourage AAC users to take their turn. With some pre-planning and preparation, they can join the conversation.

transcriptBlocks.text: Expressing feelings.
We know just how important it is for people learning to use
AAC to learn to communicate for lots of different reasons.
Sometimes we call these reasons: Communication functions.
We actually have this awesome poster that you can download
and print for free from our website.
It shows all the different reasons that we communicate. You
know, we make choices, tell stories, tell jokes and we talk
about how we feel. Expressing feelings is one of those really
important communication functions on this
poster. I often use this poster to sit with families or teachers,
depending where I am, to think about what the child might
need to work on.
I work with an AAC user called Rupert and one day
his mum and I sat down to do some planning.
He was getting really good at making choices and we'd been
working hard at telling news and giving an opinion.
And so I asked his mum: What would you think would be good
to focus on next, for Rupert's communication?
Mum said that she would love Rupert
to have a way to tell her how he feels. Sometimes when
he was upset or cranky
he might communicate this with his body and face, and Mum
might not be able to catch it in time to help problem solve
some solutions to those feelings.
So we set expressing feelings as a goal.
We put a few things in place to work on this. Firstly we started
talking about our feelings often.
We regularly told Rupert how we felt, to which he often, and
usually, rolled his eyes.. hard.
I'm not sure he cared how we felt but we did it
anyway.
Secondly, we took lots of time looking at people's faces
in books and videos and talking about how we thought they
felt. We would say things like, "Oh! She has tears coming out
of her eyes."
"She must [sad].. She must feel really sad."
I'm not sure he loved it when his mum paused the movie to
show the face of the person and talk about how they felt
but we did it anyway. And lastly and probably most importantly
we attributed meaning. We became careful observers of Rupert's
body and his face and his behaviors.
We acknowledged how we thought he might feel, and we showed
these feelings on his AAC.
So we said things like, "Oh you're rocking your body and smiling.
I think this music makes you feel happy [happy]". And "Oh dear!"
"You're banging on the table."
"I think you are [cranky]."
"I think you're feeling cranky." If we could problem-solve, we would.
Like, "Oh, I see you're [cranky].
"Oh no! Your iPad went flat."
"Let me help [help] you."
"Let's go and [charge the iPad]."
"Let's go charge the iPad". Expressing feelings with AAC didn't
come naturally to Rupert, but we continued modeling and attributing
meaning. It took a while.
It might have even been six months before Rupert
did it on his own. And then it happened. One day, Rupert
had a medical appointment on the Wednesday.
So he got up Thursday thinking it was the weekend. When Mum
showed him the schedule to say it was a school day,
I'm let's just say, he was [not happy]
He was not happy. And he showed us that he was not a happy
by stomping around and slamming doors.
He left the car without saying goodbye to mum in the morning
when she dropped him off. And then he walked into his classroom,
He pulled out his AAC, put it on his desk and he tapped
"I'm cranky."
"I'm cranky."
"I'm cranky." And of course, we kinda all cheered.
He was so confused as to why we're all so happy.
Anyway, it took ... took some time but it was worth it.
Rupert can express his feelings and tell people how he feels.
This is just such an important communication function.

Watch this video with your AAC users, model words on the AAC, write or make a shopping list and play a shopping game!

This video was from her Facebook live video on December 3rd 2020. Find us on Facebook at: https://www.facebook.com/AssistiveWare

View the on-demand training videos of our world-renowned AAC specialists https://assistivewa.re/3lr0ONu

description:
In this Facebook live, Amanda reads from Thank You, Omu! 

As families in the US get ready to celebrate Thanksgiving, this is a wonderful book to read together and remember to share what we have with others and to give thanks. 

Watch this video with your AAC users, model words on the AAC, write some thank you notes and make some soup!

This video was from her Facebook live video on November 26th 2020. Find us on Facebook at: https://www.facebook.com/AssistiveWare

View the on-demand training videos of our world-renowned AAC specialists https://assistivewa.re/3lr0ONu

This video was from her Facebook live video on November 19th 2020. Find us on Facebook at: https://www.facebook.com/AssistiveWare

title: Amanda's Facebook Live There's no such thing
description:
In this Facebook Live, Amanda reads a spooky but fun book called "There's no such thing".  Watch as she models words on her Proloquo2Go. Next she writes a list of opposite words, and plays a listening game, all while using AAC!

This video was from her Facebook live video on October 29th 2020. Find us on Facebook at: https://www.facebook.com/AssistiveWare

View the on-demand training videos of our world-renowned AAC specialists https://assistivewa.re/3lr0ONu

In this Facebook Live, Amanda does shared reading with an Animal Encyclopedia. She finds describing words on her AAC and writes an animal report. And as always, she finishes with some fun. Bring your children, their AAC and some animals and be ready for a fun session together.

This video was from her Facebook live video on October 22nd 2020. Find us on Facebook at: https://www.facebook.com/AssistiveWare

View the on-demand training videos of our world-renowned AAC specialists https://assistivewa.re/3lr0ONu

description:
In this Facebook Live, Amanda reads a fun book about dogs using the Pictello app. She also models words and sentences on Proloquo2Go. She does some writing and plays a game. This fun and interactive session will give you many ideas for using AAC in lessons, therapy and at home.

This video was from her Facebook live video on November 5th 2020. Find us on Facebook at: https://www.facebook.com/AssistiveWare

More about Proloquo2Go: https://www.assistiveware.com/products/proloquo2go

More about Pictello: https://www.assistiveware.com/products/pictello

You can convert books from Tar Heel reader so that they can be read in Pictello. Here is the link: https://www.assistiveware.com/tar-heel-reader-pictello-converter

In this Facebook Live, we join Amanda for some cooking. Amanda uses AAC (Proloquo2Go) as she checks out some recipes, writes a shopping list and finally makes a strawberry milkshake.

This video was from her Facebook live video on October 8th 2020. Find us on Facebook at: https://www.facebook.com/AssistiveWare

View the on-demand training videos of our world-renowned AAC specialists https://assistivewa.re/3lr0ONu

title: Learn how to attribute meaning with your AAC user
description:
Attributing meaning is an important communication partner skill. It allows us to connect with someone learning to use AAC. It can guide how we model with AAC.

Read more about how we can support someone learning to use AAC to communicate: https://www.assistiveware.com/learn-aac/build-communication-partner-skills

View the on-demand training videos of our world-renowned AAC specialists https://assistivewa.re/3lr0ONu

transcriptPath: /Users/mike/.vvx/transcripts/Youtube/AssistiveWare/Read a book with Proloquo2Go and Pictello.en-orig.srt
description:
Amanda and Matthew read a Pictello story together. Watch them as they talk about the book with AAC - Proloquo2Go. 

Amanda also shows us how to convert a book from Tarheel reader into Pictello. Here is the link: https://www.assistiveware.com/tar-heel-reader-pictello-converter

More about Pictello: https://www.assistiveware.com/products/pictello

More about Proloquo2Go: https://www.assistiveware.com/products/proloquo2go

This video was from her Facebook live video on October 1st 2020. Find us on Facebook at: https://www.facebook.com/AssistiveWare

View the on-demand training videos of our world-renowned AAC specialists https://assistivewa.re/3lr0ONu

description:
In this week's Facebook Live, we read the book "Say Something" by Peter H. Reynolds. Join Amanda, as she uses AAC: Proloquo2Go to model words and sentences.

This video was from her Facebook live video on September 23rd 2020. Find us on Facebook at: https://www.facebook.com/AssistiveWare

View the on-demand training videos of our world-renowned AAC specialists https://assistivewa.re/3lr0ONu

Looking for a great idea to support your AAC user in their journey to develop literacy skills? 
Watch Amanda use and model AAC to write lists! 
She shares an idea for talking about what in our lives is different and the same. 

Join our community on Facebook for more resources: https://www.facebook.com/groups/241684205905600/

View the on-demand training videos of our world-renowned AAC specialists https://assistivewa.re/3lr0ONu

View the on-demand training videos of our world-renowned AAC specialists https://assistivewa.re/3lr0ONu

Amanda shows you how you can run a Zoom session with Proloquo2Go for Mac. https://www.assistiveware.com/products/proloquo2go
Using Proloquo2Go for Mac is ideal if you are doing online therapy or educational sessions using online platforms.

Join our community on Facebook for more resources: https://www.facebook.com/groups/241684205905600/

We are all seeing and feeling new things during the Coronavirus. One of those things is: Face masks. 

Amanda uses Proloquo2Go and her core word board to explain more about face masks. Share this video with your children and students to help them understand more about face masks.

Join our community on Facebook for more resources: https://www.facebook.com/groups/241684205905600/

Make sure you are talking about the coronavirus as well: https://www.assistiveware.com/blog/using-proloquo2go-to-talk-about-the-coronavirus

title: AssistiveWare – Me and my computer
description: Elina was born with athetoid cerebral palsy. About a year ago, when she was 9 years old, she got a computer and in this 4-minute video, she demonstrates how it has revolutionized her life. The computer has given her independence as she can now draw and write by herself. She accesses her Apple iBook with an adapted joystick and uses AssistiveWare's KeyStrokes on-screen keyboard with word prediction for writing. She is also experimenting with Proloquo and the Infovox iVox voices for speech feedback while she types. At home and at school her computer means life to her! Elina lives in California, United States of America.
